'''Harry Laurence Anderson''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} is a British chemist in the Department of Chemistry, [[University of Oxford]]. He is well known for his contributions in the syntheses of [[Supramolecular chemistry|supramolecular systems]] ([[porphyrin]] [[nanoring]]s and [[nanowires]]), exploration of the extraordinary physical properties of large pi-conjugated systems, and synthesis of cyclo[18]carbon.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aay1914 |title=Cyclocarbon |journal=Science |date=20 September 2019 |doi=10.1126/science.aay1914 |last1=Kaiser |first1=Katharina |last2=Scriven |first2=L. M. |last3=Schulz |first3=F. |last4=Gawel |first4=P. |last5=Gross |first5=L. |last6=Anderson |first6=H. L. |volume=365 |issue=6459 |pages=1299–1301 |pmid=31416933 |arxiv=1908.05904 |s2cid=201019470 }}</ref> He is a Professor of Chemistry at [[Keble College, Oxford]].<ref>{{Scopus id }}</ref><ref>{{EuropePMC |ORCID =0000-0002-1801-8132}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.keble.ox.ac.uk/academics/about/professor-h-l-anderson |title=Professor Harry L. Anderson FRS — Keble College |author=<!--Not stated--> |access-date=4 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181013091134/https://www.keble.ox.ac.uk/academics/about/professor-h-l-anderson |archive-date=13 October 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Education ==
Harry Anderson studied chemistry at [[Christ Church, Oxford|Christ Church, University of Oxford]], where he received his Bachelor of Arts degree in 1987. This was followed by graduate studies under [[Jeremy Sanders]] at the [[University of Cambridge]], where he received his doctoral degree in 1990.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hla.chem.ox.ac.uk/group/harry.shtml |title=Anderson Research Group@Oxford University |author=<!--Not stated--> |access-date=4 September 2018 }}</ref>

==Career and Research ==
Anderson started his independent research as a [[research fellow]] at [[Magdalene College, Cambridge]] in 1990–1993, and conducted his research in 1993–1994 as SERC [[postdoctoral research]] fellow at [[ETH Zurich|ETH-Zürich]], Switzerland. He returned to University of Oxford in 1994 as university lecturer in organic chemistry and tutor in Keble College. In 2004, he became professor of chemistry at the University of Oxford.

Template directed syntheses ubiquitously exist in nature ([[protein biosynthesis]], etc.), which provides inspiration for synthesising artificial supramolecular systems. Using porphyrin [[monomer]]s/[[oligomer]]s and molecular templates of various sizes, porphyrin nanoring systems can be constructed with high versatility.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1002/anie.200801188| title = Enhanced π Conjugation around a Porphyrin[6] Nanoring| journal = Angewandte Chemie International Edition| volume = 47| issue = 27| pages = 4993–4996| year = 2008| last1 = Hoffmann | first1 = M. | last2 = Kärnbratt | first2 = J. | last3 = Chang | first3 = M. H. | last4 = Herz | first4 = L. M. | last5 = Albinsson | first5 = B. | last6 = Anderson | first6 = H. L. | pmid = 18506860|author4-link=Laura Herz }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1002/anie.200604601| title = Template-Directed Synthesis of a π-Conjugated Porphyrin Nanoring| journal = Angewandte Chemie International Edition| volume = 46| issue = 17| pages = 3122–3125| year = 2007| last1 = Hoffmann | first1 = M. | last2 = Wilson | first2 = C. J. | last3 = Odell | first3 = B. | last4 = Anderson | first4 = H. L. | pmid = 17318935}}</ref> These supramolecular systems also bear appealing co-ordination properties, providing inspirations for the co-ordination phenomena existing in nature.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1021/ja209254r| title = Stepwise Effective Molarities in Porphyrin Oligomer Complexes: Preorganization Results in Exceptionally Strong Chelate Cooperativity| journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society| volume = 133| issue = 51| pages = 20962–20969| year = 2011| last1 = Hogben | first1 = H. K. | last2 = Odell | first2 = B. | last3 = Claridge | first3 = T. D. W. | last4 = Anderson | first4 = H. L. | pmid=21544909}}</ref>

Vernier templating refers to the syntheses of complexes using templates and molecular building blocks with mismatching co-ordination numbers to construct larger molecular systems by incorporating more than one template molecule and more molecular building blocks than usual. Porphyrin nanoring systems are excellent examples in realising this methodology and giant artificial molecular systems with their molecular weights of small proteins can be constructed.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/nature09683| title = Vernier templating and synthesis of a 12-porphyrin nano-ring| journal = Nature| volume = 469| issue = 7328| pages = 72–75| year = 2011| last1 = o'Sullivan | first1 = M. Anderson's nomination for the [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2013|Royal Society in 2013]] reads: {{centred pull quote|Harry Anderson is known internationally for his insightful contributions to the design and synthesis of supramolecular materials and molecular wires. He has introduced new concepts for molecular design, and ground-breaking approaches to template-directed synthesis, leading to materials with unprecedented electronic and nonlinear optical characteristics. He has pioneered the investigation of conjugated porphyrin oligomers, encapsulated pi-systems, nanorings and two-photon absorbing dyes, and he has worked closely with physicists and photobiologists to understand the relationship between molecular structure and function. His work has resulted in profound insights into the factors controlling long-range electronic coupling and charge-transport in [[supramolecular]] systems.<ref name="royal"/>}}
